title: BackgroundService and Hosted Workloads
description: Implement long-running background tasks with BackgroundService, integrate with DI and logging, and learn when to use IHostedService versus worker services.

data.text: Web applications do more than respond to HTTP requests. They also process queued messages, poll external APIs, run scheduled jobs, and maintain caches. ASP.NET Core provides `IHostedService` for any background workload that starts with the application and stops when it shuts down. `BackgroundService` is a convenience base class that simplifies the most common pattern: a long-running loop with cancellation support.

Worker Services are console applications built on the Generic Host that run `BackgroundService` implementations. They can run standalone, in Docker containers, or as Windows services. Because they use the same Generic Host as ASP.NET Core, they get DI, logging, and configuration for free.

`IHostedService` is the low-level interface with `StartAsync` and `StopAsync`. You use it when you need explicit control over startup and shutdown sequencing. `BackgroundService` implements `IHostedService` and provides a single `ExecuteAsync` method that runs a loop until a cancellation token is triggered. For most long-running tasks, `BackgroundService` is the simpler and safer choice.

data.title: Polling external API with BackgroundService
data.content: A background service that polls an external API and updates a local cache.

data.text: Background services run outside the HTTP request pipeline, so there is no ambient scoped service provider. If you need scoped services like `DbContext` or `IHttpClientFactory` inside your background loop, create a new scope using `IServiceProvider.CreateScope()` for each unit of work. This ensures proper disposal and lifetime boundaries.

data.title: Always Create a Scope for Scoped Services
data.text: Never inject a scoped service directly into a BackgroundService constructor. The service is resolved from the root provider at startup and will be treated as a singleton, causing lifetime validation errors and data leakage. Always create a scope inside your loop.

The `dotnet new worker` template creates a project pre-configured for background workloads. It uses `Host.CreateApplicationBuilder`, registers your `BackgroundService`, and runs the host. You can add web endpoints to a Worker Service if needed, or run it purely as a background process.

data.title: When to use which pattern
items: Use BackgroundService for simple periodic tasks, polling loops, or queue consumers.
Use IHostedService when you need separate StartAsync and StopAsync logic without a loop.
Use a Worker Service project for standalone background applications that may run in Docker or as a Windows service.
Use ASP.NET Core with BackgroundService for background tasks that need to share a process with your web API.

terms.definition: A base class that implements IHostedService and provides an ExecuteAsync loop with built-in cancellation support.
An interface for starting and stopping background tasks with the host lifecycle.
A console application template built on the Generic Host for running background workloads without HTTP endpoints.
A scope created from IServiceProvider to resolve scoped services outside the request pipeline.

data.title: Create a Queue Processing Service
data.description: Build a BackgroundService that polls a database for pending jobs and processes them.
steps: Create a new Worker Service project using 'dotnet new worker -n JobProcessor'.
Define a Job entity and a DbContext for tracking pending and completed jobs.
Register the DbContext and a scoped IJobProcessor service.
In BackgroundService.ExecuteAsync, create a scope, resolve IJobProcessor, and poll the database for pending jobs.
Use CancellationToken to exit the loop gracefully when the host stops.
Run the service and verify jobs are processed and marked complete.
data.expectedOutcome: A production-pattern background service that safely uses scoped services within a long-running loop and handles graceful shutdown.

data.title: BackgroundService Summary
points: BackgroundService is the simplest way to run long-running background tasks in ASP.NET Core.
Always create a scope when you need scoped services inside a background loop.
IHostedService gives you explicit StartAsync and StopAsync control.
Worker Services are standalone background apps using the Generic Host.
CancellationToken lets you stop the loop gracefully when the host shuts down.
data.takeaway: Background workloads are first-class citizens in ASP.NET Core. Using BackgroundService with proper scoping and cancellation lets you build reliable background processing that integrates cleanly with the host lifecycle.
